title: NatureLM-audio: a bioacoustic model, not a nature translator
review_depth: Reviewed the ICLR 2025 proceedings abstract, architecture/training sections, BEANS-Zero tasks and evaluation, Tables 3–6, the BirdNET/Perch comparison caveat, conclusion and risk discussion. Reviewed Sections 2–4 and limitations of the 11-page arXiv v2 follow-up identified by its authors as a NeurIPS 2025 workshop paper. Checked the official overview/Quick Start, the Hugging Face model and dataset metadata, and the official code/data repository inventories and license files described in the source records. No dataset files, code or model weights were acquired, no inference was run and no results were reproduced.
finding: NatureLM-audio combines a BEATs audio encoder with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and responds to audio-plus-text prompts with outputs such as species labels, detections, call types, life-stage classes and captions. Its ICLR 2025 paper reports strong results on several BEANS-Zero tasks and evaluates held-out taxa; the paper cautions that BirdNET and Perch comparison datasets overlap their training data, so those are topline rather than fully fair comparisons. A NeurIPS 2025 workshop follow-up preprint exposes prompt-format brittleness: asking for common and scientific names together reduced accuracy to 6–12% on two benchmark components compared with prompts asking for one name. For those combined-name prompts, the authors report that LoRA interpolation at about α=0.7 raises accuracy from 6% to 45% on Watkins and 12% to 63% on CBI. Separately, on one 425-sample, 40-class closed-set unseen-family task, reported F1 rose from 0.09 to 0.28 (the authors describe this as a >200% relative improvement). These are bounded classification and instruction-following results, not evidence that the model discovers what an animal means or can hold a conversation with it. The current training-data viewer lists 26.4 million rows; the paper notes that prompt counts can derive from the same audio, so row counts are not unique recordings.
limitations: The ICLR results are benchmark-specific, and Talk2Nature has not independently reproduced them. The follow-up is a NeurIPS 2025 workshop paper/preprint, not a Talk2Nature validation; its authors state that the unseen-family closed-set result is limited in scope. Current official documentation says the v1.1 demo was updated in April 2026, while its Quick Start says performance is strongest for birds, especially in North America and Western Europe; calls above about 8 kHz (including bat calls) are outside the model frequency range; tropical regions are harder; wrong-taxon prompts are not reliably rejected; and emotion interpretation or translation beyond call-type prediction is unsupported. Several other prompted tasks are explicitly experimental. The model card identifies CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 weights with Llama 3.1 terms also applicable. The 26.4M-row training dataset and 50.5 GB BEANS-Zero dataset each display a generic “other” license at the hub; row-level training-data license values differ, and component rights were not audited. The NatureLM code repository and merging-code repository declare MIT, but that does not clear weights or datasets. The BEANS-Zero code repository had no root LICENSE at the checked URL. No files were acquired, and no model or code was run.
lesson: Treat a fluent answer as a model prediction about a defined acoustic task, not as an animal’s message. For Talk2Nature, keep the first software value in passive recording, observation, and transparent researcher review; clearly separate human-entered notes from model guesses. If a later benchmark is justified, select one labelable task, pin model and data versions, compare against simple and context-only baselines, hold out animals or sites where appropriate, test prompt sensitivity, and document each component’s license before any run. The large Llama-based model and its non-commercial weights are not a default phone or paid-product dependency.
next_review: Ask qualified bioacoustic and ML reviewers which single task and holdout unit would answer a useful project question. Reconcile training and benchmark component rights, pin exact code/model releases, and estimate compute only after a rights-cleared dataset and independent labels exist. Do not start AutoResearch until its documented data, reviewer, split, metric, locked-test, baseline and execution-boundary gates are all met.

title: When another organism responds
seo_description: A moth study shows that plant-emitted ultrasonic clicks can alter egg-laying choices, with results changing when real plants are present.
review_depth: Full version-of-record text reviewed through the NCBI PMC copy and eLife PDF, including main methods, figures, public reviewer comments and author responses. The public Mendeley Data v1 file browser was inventoried: three folders with 32 files (24 CSV, four R, two MATLAB and two XLSX). Previewed the data.xlsx headers/rows, one XY-point CSV, and part of run_stats_whole.m, which loads data.xlsx and separates experiment 3. File-information panels for data.xlsx, run_stats_whole.m and one XY-point CSV displayed CC0 1.0 and SHA-256 values; the Download All ZIP panel displayed a SHA-256. No files were downloaded, full workbooks/scripts were not inspected, code was not run, raw data were not reanalysed, and no independent specialist review was obtained.
finding: In controlled choices, female Egyptian cotton leafworm moths (Spodoptera littoralis) changed where they laid egg clusters when playback of drought-stressed tomato-plant clicks was present. The preference depended on the other cues: playback attracted oviposition in a plant-free arena, while moths preferred the silent side when healthy tomato plants were offered on both sides. Deafening removed the plant-free playback preference; male-moth click controls did not produce a detected preference. A separate long-arena experiment used a lower 30-click/min rate and found egg clusters concentrated near the playback and feeder rather than the silent edge.
limitations: This is one moth species, one plant species and a controlled laboratory/greenhouse study, not evidence that plants intentionally communicate or that animals can be translated by AI. The authors characterize drought sounds as a likely cue rather than an evolved message. The main choice experiments used 60 clicks/min; the authors measured at most 20 clicks/min from 45 drying seedlings in a 50-hour recording and argue that a dense patch could raise exposure. The later 30-click/min gradient setup differs in arena and subject design, so it is not a direct replication of the main choice trials. Preferences also reverse with plant context; other visual, olfactory and tactile cues complicate interpretation. The Mendeley inventory contains tabular and XY-point files, not listed audio recordings; it cannot serve as an animal-audio benchmark. The limited preview does not verify all file contents, joins, dependencies or the publisher ZIP's correspondence. Reviewer comments raised ecological realism, effect-size presentation, availability of raw data/code and species generalization; Talk2Nature has not independently reproduced or reanalysed the results.
lesson: A receiver's controlled response can show that a sound is a usable cue in a specific setting. That is a stronger behavioral result than detecting a signal, but it does not by itself establish a sender's intent, a shared message or conversation.
next_review: Obtain qualified insect-bioacoustics review of the experimental units and analysis. If a bounded retrieval route is verified, inspect a checksum-matched subset of the Mendeley data and code without executing unreviewed code, then reproduce one prespecified table with its true replicate structure. Keep the separate publisher ZIP metadata-only unless exact comparison is necessary and its artifact terms are verified. This is not an audio/model-training benchmark; ordinary phone microphones are not ultrasonic recorders.

title: Fungal electrical activity: a sensor study, not a decoded language
seo_description: Fungal-potential sensors recorded electrical activity in one strain. The study suggests a measurement method, not a decoded fungal language.
review_stage: Targeted primary article and dataset metadata review
review_depth: Reviewed the publisher/PMC indexed article abstract, experimental setup, selected Results and Figures 1–3, Discussion, license and data-availability statement; checked the Mendeley Data v1 landing-page description and license. The article and data pages were intermittently CAPTCHA/403 limited. Supplementary Method S1, the raw dataset files and the full per-treatment statistical tables were not inspected; no result was reproduced.
finding: Buffi et al. tested a printed fungal-potential card with embedded differential electrodes, a controlled humid chamber and Faraday cage on one Fusarium oxysporum strain. The article reports a significant 1,604% power-spectral-density increase after fungal growth connected inoculated electrodes compared with non-inoculated controls. The authors argue the setup can detect fungal-associated electrical activity and report that some treatments alter the recorded frequency patterns.
limitations: This is a laboratory sensor/method study on one strain, not an animal-style communication experiment. Extracellular voltage and frequency patterns do not identify a message, receiver, referent or semantic code. Treatment effects were mixed: the cycloheximide power change was not significant; voriconazole's increase was not significant; calcimycin's pattern matched its DMSO carrier, which likely interfered with the gold electrodes; sodium azide's temporary change also had a brief water-control anomaly. The 2024 critique and 2025 review describe unresolved measurement and interpretation challenges. The dataset page declares CC BY 4.0 but its file manifest and bytes were not reviewed; the analysis code is only identified as supplementary Method S1 and its component-specific terms were not confirmed.
lesson: Treat fungal electrophysiology as a separate sensing channel that needs laboratory electrodes, environmental controls and biological controls. Evidence of stimulus-associated activity is not evidence of language or of a phone-mediated way to talk with mushrooms.
next_review: Before any reuse, inspect the exact Mendeley file manifest and data, reproduce the documented preprocessing, and review supplementary Method S1 and its terms separately from the paper and dataset. Ask a qualified mycologist/electrophysiologist to assess replication, biological-replicate structure and electrode/solvent controls. Keep it outside the first animal benchmark and do not start model training.

title: animal2vec and MeerKAT: rare-call detection, not translation
seo_description: animal2vec and MeerKAT support rare-call detection in a large meerkat audio dataset. Their labels enable event evaluation, not translation.
review_stage: Targeted peer-reviewed methods, results and rights review
review_depth: Reviewed the 2026 published article's dataset methods, class definitions, annotation quality, evaluation design/results, discussion, ethics and data-availability statement; the official animal2vec repository and README; and the article's separate dataset, code and checkpoint license statements. The article supplement, deposited files/manifests, archived code contents and model weights were not inspected or acquired. No published result was reproduced.
finding: The peer-reviewed study presents animal2vec as a rare-event bioacoustic detector/classifier and MeerKAT as 1,068 hours of 8 kHz meerkat audio, including 184 hours with complete event labels across 66,398 ten-second samples. The paper reports eight vocalization classes and three non-call event classes, overlapping labels, millisecond event boundaries and inter-annotator timing reliability just over 10 ms. It is a valuable example of continuous audio, quiet/background intervals and event-based precision–recall evaluation.
limitations: The data combine animal-worn collars and close directional microphones, not ordinary phone recordings. The paper describes a stratified five-fold split over samples but this review did not verify that folds separate animals, days or source recordings. Public filenames are randomized and identity/time order are intentionally unavailable; the authors say these can be requested. A separate held-out-data analysis is not evidence of unseen-animal generalization. The focal label is an analyst's source attribution based partly on relative intensity, spectral change and context; it is not meaning. Predicting assigned call categories, including labels such as alarm or social call, does not demonstrate receiver comprehension or translation. Dataset and checkpoints are CC BY-NC 4.0; the code is MIT. Those rights are separate, and the data/weights are outside the project's commercial-capable path. No media, code or weights were acquired or run.
lesson: A useful first ML task can be bounded event detection with complete quiet intervals, explicit source labels and event-level metrics. It must remain separate from context inference, meaning and translation, and it needs animal/session-aware evaluation where authorized group keys exist.
next_review: Keep as a methods reference. Before any separate non-commercial reproduction, inspect the exact Edmond inventory and code archive, verify all component terms and dependencies, obtain authorized animal/session grouping metadata, and preregister a leakage-safe evaluation with a qualified reviewer.

title: Ice-crystal claims: why beautiful images need stronger tests
review_depth: Reviewed the full 2006 four-page article, full 2008 Journal of Scientific Exploration paper, Douglas Stokes’s 2009 letter (p. 83), and Kokubo, Nemoto and Kawano’s 2017 technical note (pp. 73–86). Checked the reported designs, outcomes and experimental units. The 2006 full text was read from an author-hosted copy; its indexed PubMed record remains linked. Raw photographs, original analysis files/code and a full systematic literature search were not reviewed; no independent specialist review was obtained.
finding: The 2006 pilot reports that 100 blind judges gave higher beauty ratings to 24 selected treated-condition images than to 16 control images (means 2.87 vs 1.88; one-tailed p=.001). The images came from just four bottles (two per condition), and only drops with a discernible crystal were photographed. The same investigator group’s 2008 triple-blind follow-up used six bottles (two per condition) and 300 drop photographs. Its authors reported a weak three-condition beauty effect (p=.03) and a treated-versus-proximal-control comparison at p=.05, one-tailed; the beauty effect was not significant after adjustment for image interest (p=.20), and the three-condition objective-contrast result was not significant (p=.25). These are reports by the study authors, not independent confirmation.
limitations: The 2006 image-level ratings do not create more independent treated water sources than the four bottles; the authors themselves noted different treatment/control environments, selective photographing of visible crystals and the need to assess all drops and use more objective measures. The 2008 authors modeled bottles as random effects but used only two bottles per condition. Stokes’s 2009 letter specifically critiques the 2008 treated-versus-proximal comparison: treating the four bottles as the units gives a maximum one-tailed exact rank probability of 1/6 (.167). This letter does not directly analyze the 2006 pilot. The 2017 technical note discusses dependent photographs and too few bottles; its authors also acknowledge their own judge-level tests were invalid and their two-bottle-per-condition trials too small. That small methods study is not a decisive independent null replication. No reviewed study shows that water understands words, carries a message, or reliably changes crystal structure because of thought.
lesson: Many photographs and ratings cannot substitute for independent experimental units. A communication claim also needs a defined sender and receiver, a signal, and a controlled functional response; visual resemblance or a human beauty score is not a message. This is a lesson in research design, not biological evidence or a basis for Talk2Nature machine learning.
next_review: Keep this as a methods-critical case only. Any new test would need specialist review, preregistration, many independently randomized bottle batches, blinded handling, all-drop measurement, objective outcomes, a frozen analysis and independent replication. Do not use these papers to train or benchmark an animal-communication model.

title: Parrot owners can contribute; species still matter
review_depth: Full main article text, including methods, results, discussion, data-availability and rights statements, reviewed through the Europe PMC full-text XML. Official Figshare v4 API metadata and its single-file manifest were checked. The supplementary questionnaire (Appendix 1), workbook, and raw responses were not inspected or acquired.
finding: The authors received 898 voluntary survey responses and retained a cleaned sample of 877 companion parrots across 33 genera and 73 species after quality checks and excluding birds not reported to mimic human sounds. Respondents said sampled parrots sometimes (36%) or frequently (53%) used mimicked vocalizations in appropriate human contexts without prompting. These are caregiver reports, not independently observed events or receiver tests.
limitations: Recruitment used email and social media with parrot advocacy, care, and interest groups and was explicitly biased toward birds that mimic human sounds. The survey asked respondents for their names and email addresses; although the published data item declares CC BY 4.0, the XLSX has not been inspected, so presence or absence of identifiers, consent scope, and privacy suitability are unknown. The contextual-use measure is owner-assessed, not a timestamped recording or controlled behavioral response. This dataset is not an acoustic corpus, decoded vocabulary, or validated training set.

A Talk2Nature observation flow should preserve a time-stamped observation, the caregiver's interpretation, the source recording, and any later independent review as separate fields, with species and individual uncertainty explicit.

Seek qualified parrot-communication review of a prospective observer codebook; do not admit this owner-survey table to audio-model training.

title: When companion parrots use names: what a survey can and cannot show
seo_description: A caregiver survey reports name use across companion parrots. It suggests observation questions, not an audio corpus or proof of call meaning.
review_depth: PLOS ONE article HTML reviewed for abstract, methods, results and discussion; the official correction notice was checked. Supporting information, raw survey data and figures were not downloaded or inspected, and no independent reanalysis was performed.
finding: The survey reports on 1,202 companion parrots across 89 species; phrase-use information was supplied for 884 birds, with names reported for 413. Multiple observers identified 131 reported examples of appropriate name use across 88 birds and 30 species, and 69 individualized examples across 42 birds and 19 species.
limitations: These are human survey reports about learned human-language phrases, not recordings or experiments on natural parrot calls. Context was supplied or interpreted by respondents, reports were not representative, and the authors state that scoring remained subjective and does not unequivocally demonstrate understanding. The abstract says 802 example phrases contained names while the Results section says 801; the May 2026 correction adds ORCID identifiers only. Methods say the survey requested both respondent and parrot names. The article describes its S2 phrase dataset as de-identified, but we have not inspected that workbook or independently assessed disclosure risk; review the exact files and terms before reuse.
lesson: For a simple phone workflow, keep three things distinct: a time-stamped event someone could observe, the owner's own description of context, and any later scientific interpretation. Use aliases, preserve unknowns, and never turn an owner's interpretation into a model label by default. This survey is useful for designing a participatory observation interface, not for training an audio model or claiming that parrots translate human speech.
next_review: Compare the survey's categories with controlled parrot name-use studies and ask a qualified parrot-communication researcher to review a prospective, privacy-preserving codebook before any participant data collection. A useful follow-up would test observer agreement on directly observed context separately from owner-reported interpretation.

Before any benchmark, inspect the dataset loader and exact split, obtain qualified herpetology/bioacoustics review, and define site/time generalization and rare-class metrics. title: Parrot touchscreen design must account for the bird
review_depth: Reviewed the University of Glasgow repository record and abstract, the author lab's project summary, and targeted Methods, Results and Discussion passages surfaced from the repository-hosted published PDF. The 19 MB PDF could not be fetched directly; this is not a full-paper review. Tables beyond the surfaced passages, supplements, raw data and code were not inspected.
finding: Seventeen trained pet parrots frequently multi-tapped; larger targets mattered more than spacing in a touchscreen enrichment task, not a communication test.
limitations: This was a touchscreen enrichment and motor-task study, not vocal communication, passive recording or a test of semantic understanding. Recruitment selected adult pet parrots comfortable with screens and objects and familiar with balloon-pop-style games; caregivers needed animal-training experience and time. Three birds did not reach testing within the protocol: two did not progress to stable engagement within six weeks and one showed slight aggression. The task involved training, treats, caregiver support and a specific tablet/perch setup. Outcomes and multitapping varied by bird; the pressure comparison included one bird–caregiver pair. The institutional record displays 'Data Availability Statement: No'; raw data/code access was not verified. No independent specialist review or replication has been completed.
lesson: If a future Talk2Nature tool is deliberately operated by a parrot, treat it as a separate animal-computer-interaction and welfare project. Candidate design questions include larger adjustable targets, tolerance for repeated taps, short optional tasks and a reliable voluntary exit, evaluated with qualified animal-computer-interaction and avian review. Do not infer preference, comprehension or communication from a touch pattern. This paper does not justify changing the current human-operated passive recorder or serve as an acoustic ML dataset.
next_review: Obtain a directly reviewable full paper and inspect the remaining tables and statistical details; verify whether any data or code are available and their terms. Before an animal-operated prototype, request independent animal-computer-interaction and avian-welfare review. Do not use this study as training or evaluation data for the proposed acoustic benchmark.

study_snapshot: 20 adult home-kept pet parrots were recruited; 17 reached testing after gradual training. Eligibility included screen/object comfort and prior balloon-pop-style app experience; caregivers had animal-training experience and time.

A 12-caregiver survey and five-bird pilot informed a three-month study. Birds learned a stable target-touch task over up to six weeks; two did not engage enough to progress and one showed slight aggression.

A custom Fitts-style app presented five series of five targets, split into 5–15 tasks at a time according to interest and fatigue. Birds had an exit button and a clear route away; caregivers were trained to stop on distress, and a parrot behaviorist reviewed sessions.

The app recorded target hits, movement time and touch positions; video review covered on-task behavior. Two researchers independently coded distracted versus on-task segments, with 97% reported agreement.

The authors report 4,720 target touches (8,995 including follow-on taps) across 892 series; 45.73% met their 300 ms multi-tap definition. Larger targets mattered more than spacing; the paper reports an approximate threshold near 100 pd / 26 mm on this setup, not a universal standard.
The Glasgow record lists the paper as CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and displays 'Data Availability Statement: No'. No raw dataset or software package was inspected; separate availability is unverified.

title: Budgerigar vocal and social records are not event-aligned
seo_description: A 48-bird study paired contact-call features with separate flock behavior labels; records do not align each call to an event.
review_depth: Targeted abstract and Methods passages from the primary PMC index, Dryad version/file metadata and README, official NMSU facility locator, and Dryad's reuse policy reviewed. Direct PMC page open encountered CAPTCHA. No Dryad files, raw audio, video, supplement or code were downloaded or executed.
finding: A 48-bird budgerigar study paired longitudinal contact-call features with separately coded flock social behavior, but the deposited data do not align each call with a social event.
limitations: The calls were recorded from one focal bird at a time in a sound-isolation chamber, visually but not acoustically connected to flockmates. Social interactions were recorded separately in home-flock video sessions. The Dryad file inventory lists derived call-feature tables, behavior coding, an interobserver workbook, example video and R scripts, but no original call audio. Shared group/date/block metadata may support a carefully bounded aggregate association, not event-level prediction or meaning. The design includes 12 flocks in two age classes; age and group-level confounding limit generalization. The reliability workbook and analysis scripts were not inspected.
lesson: A dataset can be multimodal in the study design yet still lack the synchronized, independently labeled events a model needs. Require a shared clock and source-file linkage between sound and observed behavior; group or date overlap alone is not event alignment. Treat this Dryad deposit as a protocol/schema comparator, not the first Talk2Nature context benchmark.
next_review: If aggregate vocal-learning/sociality analysis is considered, inspect the interobserver assessment, exact file/date/block joins and missingness, and predefine a flock-held-out question with a collaborator. For call-level context prediction, seek synchronized recordings with independent event annotations and access to the original audio.
expert_review: Not yet independently reviewed by an avian bioacoustics or social-behavior specialist.
study_snapshot: Does adult age relate to contact-call learning and social integration? The study addresses vocal learning and sociality, not call translation.
48 adult male budgerigars formed 12 novel flocks of four birds: six young-adult and six older-adult flocks. The experiment ran from December 2020 through April 2021.

Each bird had four 55-minute baseline sessions and 16 sessions after joining a flock. Calls were recorded individually in a sound-isolation chamber; nearby flockmates were visible but not acoustically connected.

Flock video was collected in two 80-minute sessions per recording block. Early-morning videos were sampled continuously for social interactions during a 40-minute window after a 30-minute settling period.

The February 2024 Dryad version is 68.14 MB and includes contact-call feature tables, social-interaction coding, proximity data, an interobserver-assessment workbook, example video and R scripts. The file inventory does not list original call WAV files.

The article lists CC BY 4.0. Dryad's reuse guide says its datasets use CC0; that dataset policy does not clear the article or separately included software. No deposit files were downloaded or re-distributed.

title: MammAlps aligns animal sound with video-annotated behavior
seo_description: MammAlps links wildlife audio with video-annotated behavior to evaluate visible actions, not vocal meaning.
review_depth: Targeted review of arXiv v2 sections 3.1–3.4, 5, 7.1 and 9.1–9.2; exact Zenodo v3 metadata, README, file inventory and dataset license; official CVPR Open Access indexed excerpts from the main paper and supplementary section A.1; official GitHub README, evaluation interface and LICENSE.md. The direct CVF paper and supplement fetch returned 403, so only targeted indexed excerpts were reviewed for the published version. Other supplementary methods and archive contents were not reviewed; no data or code were downloaded or run.
finding: MammAlps provides a real multimodal wildlife behavior benchmark: animal-centered video clips have matched audio and scene maps, with visible behavior labels assigned by two annotators. It evaluates observable actions and activities, not vocal meaning or animal translation.
limitations: Five wild mammal species were recorded at three sites in the Swiss National Park over six weeks; the authors withhold the exact site locations. Collection dates conflict across versions: the arXiv v2 and official CVPR main text say June–August 2023, while the arXiv/CVPR supplementary section 7.1/A.1 and Zenodo v3 say August–October 2023. The conflict persists in the published version; direct CVF fetches returned 403 and only indexed excerpts were reviewed. The period is unresolved and is not used in the atlas timeline. The published split holds out days, not verified animal identities; cross-day individual independence is unestablished. Reviewed passages describe two annotators and an unknown class but do not establish inter-annotator agreement statistics or that labeling was audio-blind. The authors acknowledge subjective behavior categories and geographic/time limits. Version 3's full data archive is 87.9 GB. Dataset terms are CC BY-NC 4.0, which excludes Talk2Nature's commercial-capable benchmark path. No audio alignment, labels, model weights, preprocessing or published result were independently reproduced.
lesson: This is a strong design comparator for testing whether sound adds predictive information beyond video, scene context and simple baselines. A behavior label is still not a message: define the prediction target, label provenance, modality ablations and grouped test before training.
next_review: Keep as a noncommercial methods reference. Before any separately approved academic reproduction, inspect the exact v3 files and dense annotations, cross-day identity structure, label reliability, event/group leakage, code and checkpoint terms, compute and storage needs. For Talk2Nature's first commercial-capable benchmark, continue seeking permissively reusable synchronized recordings with independently observed behavior labels or prepare a reviewed passive protocol.

Nine camera traps across three sites in the Swiss National Park recorded six weeks of footage. Collection dates conflict across versions: the arXiv/CVPR main text says June–August 2023; the supplement and Zenodo v3 say August–October 2023. Animal-centered video clips are paired with the matching audio and a scene-segmentation modality. Two annotators labeled visible actions and higher-level activities; unknown is available when behavior cannot be identified. The reviewed text does not establish annotator agreement or audio blinding.

The published Benchmark I split is random at the day level with label-distribution matching. This is not evidence of unseen-animal generalization. Authors report modality ablations and three-run results; their baseline training used four A100 GPUs. Talk2Nature did not reproduce those results.

Zenodo version 3 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15588220) lists an 87.9 GB archive and a 13.5 MB dense-annotation file. The dataset is CC BY-NC 4.0; the official evaluation-code repository separately declares MIT. Neither component was acquired. No model-weight license was reviewed.

title: Parrotlet babbling is vocal development, not call translation
seo_description: Green-rumped parrotlet nestlings babble as their vocal repertoires develop; this is evidence about development, not call translation.
review_depth: Targeted PMC-indexed excerpts of the primary paper's abstract, conclusion and data-access statement; the exact Dryad dataset landing page, public API dataset/version/file records (v6, version record 180872), current End User Terms and Publication Policies; and an indexed excerpt from the official KBA location factsheet. Dryad's published policy states accepted datasets are made public under CC0, with no separate exception shown on this record. API file metadata supplied exact IDs, sizes and SHA-256 digests. An unauthenticated byte-range request to the API download route returned 401; the web file stream returned HTML rather than the file. No paper PDF, supplement, dataset file or audio was downloaded or fully reviewed.
finding: The study reports vocal babbling and repertoire development in free-ranging green-rumped parrotlet nestlings of both sexes. The paper describes a corticosterone-related repertoire difference and says the babbling repertoire was not yet integrated into functional contexts; this is developmental biology, not evidence of call translation.
limitations: One wild species and a nestling developmental stage were studied at Hato Masaguaral in Guárico, Venezuela, during 2017–2018. The current Dryad API lists version 6 with 2.56 GB of audio bouts, a 43.91 MB spreadsheet of spectrographic measurements and a 4.75 KB README; per-file sizes and SHA-256 values are recorded in the resource catalog. The study includes corticosterone supplementation, so it is not a purely passive observation dataset. The README bytes, measurement schema, individual/session joins, label provenance, audio-video synchronization, treatment groups, split design and model performance were not inspected. No receiver-response or controlled semantic-decoding result is established by the reviewed material. Dryad's current terms and policy state that published datasets are made public under CC0, and no record-specific exception is displayed; this dataset-level license evidence does not establish scientific fit, privacy/welfare suitability or model admission. The article reuse license is separate and was not verified.
lesson: Parrot vocal development is a useful research direction and can help define age-aware questions, but a changing repertoire or hormone-associated difference is not a message. Preserve developmental stage, treatment and individual/session structure before considering any acoustic analysis. Do not use this archive as evidence for general parrot communication or as the first context benchmark.

title: Natural-language prompts can retrieve annotated wildlife videos
seo_description: Prompting-MammAlps tests text search over visible-behavior labels in wildlife video. It does not translate animal signals.
year_label: arXiv v1 posted July 10, 2026; official code README lists ECCV 2026
review_depth: Targeted review of arXiv v1 sections 1, 3.1–3.2, 4–7 and supplement S1.1–S1.3; official EPFL project page; pinned Hugging Face dataset card; official GitHub README, pyproject, SALMA README, repository root inventory and checkpoint issue. No dataset, code, article or model weights were acquired; no code or result was run.
finding: Prompting-MammAlps tests whether natural-language queries can retrieve camera-trap videos whose structured, visible-behavior annotations satisfy each query. The 135 ecology-informed queries include multi-attribute, multi-animal and temporal relations. This is a text interface to a video-label schema, not translation of animal signals or a two-way communication system.
limitations: The benchmark is video-only and covers seven Alpine mammal species, three sites in one Swiss national park, 15 camera views and two non-overlapping seasons (2023 and 2024); it is not a parrot or audio benchmark. The published split is by acquisition day, not verified individual identity, and cross-season distribution shift is reported. Query/video matches are built from ground-truth annotations; independent label-reliability review was not performed here. The authors report set-based F1: SALMA plus the query agent scores 0.34 across all 135 queries and 0.37 on the 113 without video-comparison prompts; zero-shot InternVideo2.0 scores 0.18 only on those 113. The commonly repeated 34% vs 18% figures therefore do not compare identical query sets. An oracle query agent on ground-truth annotations scores 0.87, so retrieval quality depends strongly on the upstream perception/annotation layer. No result was independently reproduced. Dataset terms are CC BY-NC 4.0, the code repository has no declared license, and no SALMA checkpoint release was found.
lesson: Natural-language retrieval can make an explicit behavior schema easier to explore, but it does not turn labels into an animal's message. For Talk2Nature, measure label extraction, prompt interpretation and retrieval separately; retain uncertainty, compare against simple baselines and test held-out individuals/sites before considering model training.
next_review: Keep metadata-only as a non-commercial retrieval-method comparator. Before any academic reproduction, resolve the dataset download handle, audit the exact split and label provenance, confirm code and model-weight rights, and test cross-year/site generalization. For the first Talk2Nature benchmark, continue seeking rights-cleared synchronized audio and independently timed behavior labels. AutoResearch remains NOT READY.

study_snapshot: Can text queries retrieve clips whose structured visual annotations satisfy a visible species, behavior, weather or temporal relation? The target is video retrieval, not acoustic meaning.

MammAlps-S2 contains 2,865 camera-trap video clips, 18.4 hours across 15 views, from three sites and two field seasons (2023–2024). The benchmark has 135 queries across seven mammal species, 23 actions and 12 activities; 775 videos form the test candidates.

The paper says queries were developed with a behavioral ecologist and matched to video sets using the ground-truth annotations. Exact matching excludes partial matches and retains queries with no matching video. Label reliability was not independently audited in this review.

The published split groups by acquisition day, not verified individual identity. Set-based F1 is reported per query. The 0.34 SALMA+agent result covers 135 queries; the 0.18 zero-shot InternVideo2.0 comparison covers 113 queries without video-comparison prompts. The paper also reports 0.87 for an oracle query agent applied to ground-truth annotations. None of these results was reproduced by Talk2Nature.

The dataset card declares CC BY-NC 4.0. The code repository has no GitHub license metadata or root LICENSE file; code use is unresolved. The SALMA checkpoint package was not found and a public issue asks about a future release. No dataset, code or weights were acquired.

Keep as a methods comparator for transparent retrieval over explicit labels. Do not call it animal communication, put it in a commercial-capable corpus, or treat its video-only output as audio meaning.

title: Fruit-bat calls and context: a rich dataset, not a translation key
year_label: Data descriptor and follow-up study years
review_stage: Targeted primary literature, dataset and rights review
review_depth: Reviewed the 2017 Scientific Data article's abstract, methods, data records, Tables 3–4, technical validation, usage and rights sections; the 2016 Scientific Reports results and classification methods; the 2023 iScience abstract, dataset description, sequence-HMM methods/results, discussion and data statement; the Mendeley Data version 3 description/license and official version 1/2 and 2/3 comparisons; the Mendeley public file-list API documentation and one anonymous version 3 request (HTTP 401; documentation specifies OAuth2); the NLM catalog entry; and direct public Figshare API metadata for archive item 4556074, annotation item 4555903, FileInfo item 4555897 and Metadata.pdf item 4555900. Acquired only the 3.29 MB annotation table with verified size/MD5 for aggregate-only schema/category-count comparison, plus the 367,257-byte metadata PDF for visual review of all five pages; its source API supplies no MD5, so the receipt's SHA-256 is local provenance only. No audio/video, FileInfo.csv, code or model weights were inspected, and no published model result was reproduced.
seo_description: A bat vocalization dataset links calls to observed behavior, but it is not a translation key. Animal/session splits remain unverified.
finding: The 2017 archive describes 293,238 Egyptian fruit-bat WAV files recorded at 250 kHz and 16-bit, plus 91,080 labels derived from synchronized video, including caller, addressee, behavior and social context. The data descriptor reports a post-hoc recheck of 435 annotations, with a 4% estimated context-label error rate (95% CI 2.2–5.8%). The reviewed metadata PDF says annotation FileIDs map to FileInfo.csv; its tables describe recording-date ranges, treatment/channel settings and bats that recur across treatments, and define known, unknown and ambiguous caller/receiver codes. This makes a file/animal grouping audit plausible, but not yet verified against FileInfo rows.
limitations: The 2016 analysis reported 61% balanced accuracy for four aggressive contexts versus 25% chance, using 14,863 calls from seven adult females. Its vocalization-level cross-validation does not establish generalization to held-out bats. The 2023 follow-up used sequences from three adult females; the context HMM used 326 sequences (2,953 syllables), formed 12,900 n-grams and reported overall balanced accuracy 66 ± 10 under random eight-fold cross-validation. Shuffling syllable order left the score unchanged. These are predictions of observer-coded context, not evidence that bats or humans interpret a call as a message. The 2023 authors say behavioral experiments are needed to establish biological relevance. The laboratory archive used synchronized video, isolated chambers and specialized 250 kHz ultrasound recording; ordinary phone recordings cannot be assumed to match its bandwidth, calibration or capture conditions. The Figshare public item API declares CC0 1.0 for archive item 4556074 and lists one 3,049,199,327-byte ZIP; its payload and embedded rights notices were not inspected. The separate annotation item 4555903 declares CC0 1.0; its 3,286,405-byte file was locally size/MD5 verified. The aggregate audit found 91,080 rows, 87,986 distinct file IDs, no malformed fields and exact Table 4 count matches. These are structural/transcription checks, not independent validation. The PDF does not prove FileInfo row coverage, uniqueness or actual joins; the 31,574,701-byte FileInfo.csv was not fetched. Its API record has no upstream MD5 and the file exceeds the collector's 5 MiB per-file ceiling. Multiple annotations can belong to one file; ambiguous/unknown identities are present. No raw rows are published. No audio, video, FileInfo contents, encodings, code or weights were inspected or run.
lesson: This work offers a strong template for linking sound to independently observed context, auditing annotation uncertainty, and separating acoustic prediction from receiver comprehension. For a new benchmark, split by animal and session, keep context-only and background controls, audit duplicate calls and channels, and reserve receiver-response experiments for a separate hypothesis.
next_review: The 3.05 GB audio/video archive remains metadata-only and is not required for this bounded audit. First determine with a qualified bat-bioacoustics reviewer whether acquiring FileInfo.csv is necessary and define a bounded integrity plan for its missing upstream MD5; if justified, inspect only schema, key coverage, duplicate FileIDs, recording times/channels and links to the already audited annotation aggregate. Then test whether animal- and session-grouped splits can be formed without cross-group leakage. Keep annotations out of training unless an independently reviewed protocol and fit-for-purpose benchmark are approved. title: Wild parrot duet structure: sequence patterns, not decoded meaning
seo_description: Wild yellow-naped amazons show flexible duet sequences, but the study could not confidently assign meanings to calls or duets.
kind: Wild vocal-sequence study and dataset review
review_stage: Targeted primary article, dataset metadata and reuse-rights review
review_depth: Reviewed the publisher article HTML for its abstract, sites and recordings, call categorization, acoustic analyses, syntax methods and results, discussion, data-availability statement and supplementary-file inventory. Reviewed the full Dryad dataset landing page and README description and Dryad’s current reuse-rights guide. The workbook and publisher supplements were not downloaded or inspected; no published analysis was reproduced.
finding: The study examined warble duets from 13 mated pairs of wild yellow-naped amazons in north-west Costa Rica during 2006–2008. The authors report creating 1,136 duet files; 52 high-quality warble duets from 12 pairs were used in the syntax analysis. They report recurring call types, flexible ordering, 19 positive and four negative call-type associations, while most complete duet sequences were unique. This is evidence of measurable sequence structure in this study, not a translated conversation.
limitations: Analysis-specific sample counts differ: the initial lexicon is described as 469 calls from 54 duets and 13 pairs, while syntax analysis used 52 duets from 12 pairs. Methods describe 36 multi-example call types plus 11 one-time forms grouped as “Unknown”; results report 36 call types and three variants. The reported 92% repeatability came from two supervised undergraduate scorers scoring 15 hidden duets three times; it is not independent external validation. Calls could overlap and be difficult to segment, and sex assignment relied on established duet-order rules. Quadratic discriminant analysis and naive Bayes did not classify the full call-type set; pairwise naive Bayes separated only two similar types. Syntax/collocation is not semantic decoding: the authors state that they cannot confidently assign meanings to calls, collocates or duets and discuss possible territory-defense functions. Recordings used a tripod-mounted directional microphone and video, not ordinary phone capture. The species is described as Critically Endangered, so this atlas uses country-scale geography only. Dryad lists a small measurements workbook, not raw audio; the publisher separately lists a WAV and two DOCX supplements whose terms and contents were not reviewed. The specific article reuse license was not established. No Talk2Nature specialist review, independent replication or model result exists.
lesson: For Talk2Nature, represent pair or individual identity, ordered event positions, timing, overlap, uncertain caller identity and annotation provenance separately. Preserve “unknown” and distinguish a next vocal event from a response. Keep sequence structure, context association and experimentally demonstrated meaning as different evidence levels. This wild-species study is a methods comparator; it does not establish that household phone recordings are suitable or change the provisional companion-parrot pilot.
next_review: Keep this as a metadata-only methods reference, outside the first ML benchmark. Before considering the workbook, review the exact rows and pair identifiers under a specialist-led sensitive-species and research-use assessment; evaluate article and supplementary-file terms separately. A future question should test whether independent annotators can agree on call boundaries and speaker/overlap labels before comparing acoustic baselines. AutoResearch remains NOT READY.

title: A parrot can imitate a call to address another bird. What the experiment shows.
seo_description: A controlled conure study links targeted call imitation to receiver responses; it does not establish human-like translation or justify app playback.
taxon: Orange-fronted conure (Eupsittula canicularis; the 2012 paper uses Aratinga canicularis)
review_depth: Reviewed the full primary PLOS article text for the abstract, introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, Ethics Statement and article license. finding: Balsby, Momberg and Dabelsteen tested whether a call resembling one of two paired birds would selectively affect that bird. They studied 36 temporarily captive wild conures from 27 flocks. After exclusions, 44 of 72 trial periods were analyzed. Targeted birds responded with higher call rates and shorter latency overall, while some non-target responses were also recorded. The authors interpret this as evidence that vocal imitation can address a specific individual in this species and setting.
study_snapshot: 36 wild-caught orange-fronted conures from 27 flocks, placed in 18 pairs in outdoor aviaries for a short-term study.
A recorded contact-call loop was selected to resemble one of the two birds; each pair received four randomized trials.
Audio and video were used to count calls, estimate response latency and identify callers across the small social network.
44 of 72 trial periods were retained after exclusions for uncertain caller identity or outside-bird interactions.
The paper reports following Animal Behaviour Society guidelines and holding local research and CITES permits.
expert_review: This Talk2Nature synthesis has not received independent review by an avian communication specialist.
limitations: This was a controlled playback study of 36 wild-caught orange-fronted conures from 27 flocks, paired in short-term outdoor aviaries during 2007. Of 72 trial periods, 44 were retained for analysis after caller-assignment and outside-interaction exclusions. The authors report higher call rates and shorter response latency for the targeted bird overall, with a sex-specific call-rate pattern; non-target birds also responded. This supports a bounded, context-specific receiver response to acoustically targeted imitation, not decoding of sentence meaning, general conversation, or a result transferable to pet parrots, other species or phone speakers. The experiment used captured birds, repeated playback and video observation under research permits. No Talk2Nature replication or independent specialist review exists.
lesson: A receiver response can support a narrow claim about signal function in a defined context without revealing semantic content. The study also shows why a focal bird cannot always be analyzed alone: non-target flock members may respond. For our app, playback is an intervention, not a harmless conversational interface. Keep public tools passive; any later playback experiment needs qualified scientific and animal-welfare review, a defined protocol and relevant permits.

review_request.title: Independent methods review requested
review_request.summary: We invite a qualified bat bioacoustics or animal-behavior researcher to assess the generalization claim and the minimum evidence needed to audit it. This is a review of a published context-prediction method, not a claim about call meaning or a Talk2Nature model.
questions: What should the held-out unit be for the stated target: a new emitter, a new receiver, an unseen interacting pair, a social group, a session, or a combination? What claim does each split support?

What evidence is needed to verify that all relevant participant roles and repeated recordings are isolated across the reported development/test folds? Which dates, channels, treatments, chambers or recording sessions could confound generalization?
Are context-only, class-prior, recording-channel/background and shuffled-label baselines adequate for this question? What uncertainty estimate respects repeated animals, pairs and sessions?
What is the smallest lawful, technically sound metadata check that could resolve the key uncertainty? Is the separate FileInfo.csv actually necessary, given its size and missing upstream checksum?
review_request.status: No independent specialist review has been received. The study's exact fold files remain unavailable to this review; the full-table aggregate is not the paper subset and does not verify its splits.

limitations: The paper’s subject-independent test split is a positive reported safeguard, but Talk2Nature has not inspected the partitions or verified which identities, roles, sessions, dates, microphones, chambers or treatments cross folds. The training/validation split inside each development set ignores identity. Confidence intervals bootstrap individual predictions rather than clustered animals or sessions. Class frequencies are unequal and grooming recall is zero. Context is an observer-coded group/action category, not a test of receiver interpretation. The author-profile search is bounded. The pinned Earth Species notebook snapshot predates the EUSIPCO paper and therefore is not its promised release; a separate coauthor/lab/archive release may still exist. The repository root inventory has no visible LICENSE, and notebook 99a states code license “to be linked”; it declares dataset CC BY 4.0, which is not reconciled with Talk2Nature’s direct item-level Figshare records or derived archive-copy provenance. No independent reproduction or specialist review exists. The paper reports ImageNet-pretrained vision weights, not a bioacoustic foundation model. The arXiv v1 manuscript declares CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; proceedings-copy reuse terms were not separately reviewed. The identity graph covers the complete annotation table, not the 35,074 records used by the 2024 paper, and cannot establish whether its three folds isolate all interacting bats, emitters only, sessions, channels, treatments or chamber backgrounds. Metadata.pdf provides treatment and subject context, but the necessary per-file timestamp/channel join is in a separate 31,574,701-byte FileInfo.csv item with no upstream MD5; it was not fetched. The aggregate graph is not an independent split or leakage test.
lesson: The reported animal-held-out test split is a useful design target, but must be inspectable and audited by all caller/addressee identities, sessions, files, dates, channels and treatments. A 2021 archive-preparation notebook can clarify FileID-to-file joins without proving that FileInfo.csv is necessary for an unrelated later paper split audit. The Earth Species loader’s shuffled row-level split evaluates emitter identity rather than unseen-animal context prediction; the mini archive drops context labels. Compare acoustic models with class-prior, context-only and background/chamber baselines, use group-aware uncertainty, and keep prediction distinct from translation or comprehension. Because an interaction has two participant fields and uncertainty markers, a subject-independent claim should specify whether the split holds out emitters, both interacting animals, or another unit; it should also account for recording period, treatment/chamber and channel. Source tables make those checks possible in principle but do not prove the reported folds.

If a reviewer confirms FileInfo is necessary, first make a bounded integrity plan for its 31.6 MB file with no upstream MD5; join only the needed file/time/channel metadata and report exclusions and leakage tests. Do not train or claim reproduction until exact partitions, rights, labels, groups, baselines, metrics, a locked test and safe execution are independently reviewable.

title: BioCPPNet separates overlapping calls—it does not decode them

finding: BioCPPNet is a supervised source-separation pipeline, an audio-cleanup step rather than a communication decoder. The study constructs mixtures by additively combining known individual vocalizations, then trains a lightweight U-Net to estimate separated waveforms. It evaluates macaque, dolphin and Egyptian-fruit-bat material. For bats, the paper reports 31,399 calls from 15 highly represented individuals, with 12 used in a closed-speaker regime and three held for an open-speaker evaluation. It reports bat validation SI-SDR 9.7 and downstream caller-identity accuracy 57.5% for the closed-speaker setting; the open-speaker SI-SDR is reported as 10.0. Those results concern reconstruction and identity on generated mixtures, not behavior, context meaning, receiver comprehension or conversation.
study_snapshot: Separate two or three overlapping animal-call streams into estimated source waveforms.
The paper synthetically adds individually annotated vocalizations or vocalization streams to create mixtures with known source waveforms.

The reported bat material uses calls from 15 individuals: 12 for the closed-speaker regime and three for the open-speaker test. The model is evaluated with SI-SDR and a downstream individual-identity classifier.

The paper links macaque and Egyptian-fruit-bat datasets; dolphin recordings were provided under license and are not public. Article terms are CC BY 4.0, while implementation-code terms were not visible in the reviewed repository root.
expert_review: This Talk2Nature synthesis has not received independent review by a bioacoustic source-separation specialist.
limitations: The mixtures are constructed from known isolated source recordings, so the reported experiment does not by itself validate performance on naturally recorded, uncontrolled field mixtures. SI-SDR and caller-identity accuracy are reconstruction proxies, not evidence that a model identified call purpose or meaning. The bat open-speaker test uses three held-out individuals from the selected subset, and Talk2Nature has not reproduced the pipeline or audited source/session overlap. The repository has no visible LICENSE at the reviewed commit, so implementation reuse is not cleared. Dataset, source audio, generated mixtures, model weights and paper terms remain separate; dolphin data are explicitly restricted. No independent reproduction or expert review exists.
lesson: Keep the analysis stages distinct: detection, overlap separation, caller/source attribution, observable context association, and experimentally supported receiver response answer different questions. Source separation could make later observation or annotation more usable, but it cannot turn an acoustic stream into a translated sentence. Any future Talk2Nature separation module needs licensed inputs, known-source synthetic fixtures, a rights-cleared model/code path and evaluation against natural field recordings before public claims.
next_review: Ask a qualified bioacoustics reviewer whether source separation addresses a real bottleneck in the project's selected species and phone-recording workflow. Before implementation reuse, verify the exact repository license and inspect code/data/model provenance under a bounded, non-installing review. If pursued, first define a rights-cleared synthetic-mixture evaluation with source checksums, fixed splits, SI-SDR plus downstream utility and failure cases; this technical rehearsal must remain separate from any semantic-communication claim. title: Can trees talk through fungi? What mycorrhizal networks show
seo_description: Mycorrhizal networks may connect plant roots, but tree communication needs separate tests of signal transfer, receiver response and ecological effect.
review_stage: Targeted publisher-source review; not a systematic review
review_depth: Reviewed the Nature publisher record and surfaced article passages plus its author correction; the New Phytologist summary and selected discussion; and the full publisher-hosted Frontiers Opinion, including its article type and author statements. The underlying studies, supplementary files and data were not reanalyzed, and no specialist review was obtained.
finding: A common mycorrhizal network describes fungal hyphae shared by roots of two or more plants; such connections have been documented in particular systems, while their prevalence and functions remain debated. Whether material moves through them, whether that movement changes a receiver, and whether information is communicated are separate questions. Karst, Jones and Hoeksema (2023) warn that popular and scientific claims about widespread forest networks and beneficial “mother tree” transfers can outrun the evidence and report positive citation bias. Henriksson et al. (2023) argue that isotope studies do not yet establish significant net carbon transfer through these networks that benefits recipients, and discuss alternative pathways. Simard, Ryan and Perry (2025) respond that multiple methods support network connections and context-dependent transfer in forests. This published disagreement is a reason to state the evidence level precisely, not to declare either that networks never occur or that trees have a demonstrated shared language.
limitations: This debate is especially about forest ecology and ectomycorrhizal systems; it does not settle every plant–fungus relationship. A fungal connection or isotope transfer is not by itself evidence that one plant sent information another received. The 2025 response is explicitly an Opinion by researchers involved in this field, not an independent replication. One author of the 2023 New Phytologist review disclosed a financial interest in an organic-fertilizer company. The linked primary studies and their methods were not exhaustively reviewed here.
lesson: Keep the claims on separate rungs: demonstrate the fungal connection; trace the material and route; measure an independent receiver response; test whether a sender-derived signal explains that response better than soil, water, root, stress or other pathways. Do not call resource movement a conversation without evidence of information transfer and receiver-specific effect.

limitations: The recording-level split supports a held-out-recording interpretation, but the article does not state that individual animals are held out; the repository's YEAR+TAPENAME grouping guidance also does not prove individual separation. Edmond metadata lists a public 522.0 MB V2.0 archive, but its internal contents and split files remain unreviewed, and the deposit is described as target/noise data rather than the paper's separate call-type corpus. Edmond requires acceptance of its terms and the dataset license before download; the current Terms of Use page was not accessible and none was accepted. Metrics and supplementary split tables were not reproduced or independently checked. The work does not show one zero-shot model that translates across species, and it is not evidence of companion-parrot or phone-microphone performance.
lesson: For an app, treat any future detector or call-type output as a reviewable hypothesis and keep it separate from what the person observed. A staged detector can help find candidate sounds; it cannot answer what the animal is communicating.
